SC-001 states "The percentage of videos retained after filtering is measured against the hypothesized target of [deferred] discard rate." The placeholder `[deferred]` provides no concrete target, making the success criterion unmeasurable.
SC-005 mentions "The total training time ... is measured against a predefined time limit" but never defines what that time limit is, so the criterion cannot be evaluated.

FR-003 requires discarding the bottom [deferred] of videos based on the physics consistency score. The placeholder `[deferred]` leaves the discard proportion undefined, rendering the requirement unverifiable.
FR-006 specifies a power requirement (≥ 0.80 at effect size d = 0.5) but does not state the required sample size or how it will be computed, so the test cannot be confirmed as satisfied.

SC-002 says the physical consistency score will be measured against the PhysisForcing baseline but does not define the exact metric or threshold for comparison, leaving the success condition ambiguous.

FR-006 specifies a Two One‑Sided Tests (TOST) equivalence test with a 15 % margin, power ≥ 0.80 and effect size d = 0.5, but the original idea only called for a paired‑t test and gave no justification for these parameters. This adds a new statistical framework not requested by the idea, constituting over‑reach and a potential drift in the research question.

FR-008 requires validation of the PyBullet filter against an independent physics engine (MuJoCo) to ensure non‑circular correlation. The idea never mentioned such a validation step, so this requirement is beyond the scope of the original proposal.

FR-009 mandates physics‑preserving data augmentation when the curated set falls below 30 samples. The idea did not include any augmentation strategy; introducing it changes the data generation pipeline and may affect the independence assumptions of the planned statistical test.

FR-007 calls for a concrete CPU‑only audit task (e.g., a script asserting `torch.cuda.is_available() is False`). The idea only required that the system run on a CPU‑only environment but did not specify an explicit audit, making this an unrequested feature.
SC-005 adds a training‑time limit (≤ 6 h on a free‑tier GitHub Actions runner). The original idea never set a runtime budget, so this success criterion extends the scope beyond what was proposed.

SC-006 requires computing a Pearson/Spearman correlation < 0.95 between the PyBullet filter and a MuJoCo validator. This analysis was not part of the idea and introduces an additional validation metric not originally requested.

The validation step re‑uses the same PyBullet physics filter that was used to curate the training dataset (FR‑002/FR‑003). Evaluating the trained model by requiring ≥80 % of its generated videos to pass the *initial* PyBullet continuity check is circular: the outcome (filter pass rate) is not independent of the predictor (filter‑based data selection), so the test cannot demonstrate that the model has learned physical consistency beyond the filter’s bias.

FR‑006 specifies a TOST equivalence test with a 15 % margin, power ≥ 0.80, and effect size d = 0.5, but provides no principled justification for these choices. Without a domain‑specific rationale (e.g., prior work, clinical relevance, or a sensitivity analysis), the equivalence margin and effect size are arbitrary, risking under‑powered or over‑conservative conclusions.

R‑Bench and PAI‑Bench are adopted as proxies for ‘physical consistency’ without any argument or citation establishing construct validity. The specification does not explain why scores on these benchmarks reliably reflect the physics‑consistency property the project aims to improve, making the core claim empirically ungrounded.
